title: CUET Political Science Test 13
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Not an agency of the UN
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an agency of the United Nations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Amnesty International
Why: Amnesty International is a non-governmental organisation.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are UN agencies.
Key point: NGOs like Amnesty work alongside but outside the UN system.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Ayodhya, Shah Bano and the BSP — spot the error
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Supreme Court decided the Shah Bano case in 1985.
(B) In 1986, the Faizabad district court ordered the locks of the disputed structure to be opened.
(C) The disputed structure at Ayodhya was demolished in December 1992.
(D) Kanshi Ram founded the Janata Dal.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: Kanshi Ram founded the BSP, not the Janata Dal.
Why not the others: (A) Shah Bano was decided in 1985. (B) The locks were opened in 1986. (C) The demolition took place in December 1992. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The Janata Dal was formed in 1988 under V.P. Singh.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Year SAARC was set up
questions.question: SAARC was established in ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1985
Why: SAARC was set up in 1985 by the South Asian states.
Why not the others:
(A) 1971 is the year of the Bangladesh war.
(C) 1991 saw no such founding.
(D) SAFTA was signed in 2004.
Key point: SAARC is South Asia's main regional body.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: UN body where each member has one vote
questions.question: In the UN, the ________ is the body in which every member state has one vote.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) General Assembly
Why: All members sit in the General Assembly, each with one vote.
Why not the others:
(A) The Council has only 15 members.
(C) The Secretariat is an administrative body.
(D) The Court is made up of judges.
Key point: The General Assembly is the UN's most democratic organ.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: What happened to the ruble under shock therapy
questions.question: One effect of shock therapy in Russia was that:
options: A) the ruble became the world's main reserve currency
B) the ruble was replaced by the US dollar by law
C) the value of the ruble stayed fixed by the state
D) the value of the ruble fell sharply amid high inflation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) the value of the ruble fell sharply amid high inflation
Why: The ruble lost much of its value as inflation soared, wiping out people's savings.
Why not the others:
(A) The ruble never had that role.
(B) Russia kept the ruble.
(C) Prices and the currency were freed, not fixed.
Key point: Shock therapy brought economic ruin to many Russians.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: First popularly elected President of Russia
questions.question: ________ was elected President of Russia in 1991 and led its break from the USSR.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Boris Yeltsin
Why: Boris Yeltsin was elected President of Russia in 1991.
Why not the others:
(B) Gorbachev was the last Soviet leader.
(C) Brezhnev died in 1982.
(D) Stalin died in 1953.
Key point: Yeltsin led Russia out of the Soviet Union.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Why the US carries great weight in the UN
questions.question: One reason the US has great influence within the UN is that it:
options: A) is the single largest contributor to the UN budget
B) can veto the election of General Assembly members
C) appoints the judges of the International Court alone
D) is the only state allowed to send peacekeepers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) is the single largest contributor to the UN budget
Why: The US pays the largest share of the UN budget, which gives it great leverage.
Why not the others:
(B) No such veto exists.
(C) The judges are elected by the UN.
(D) Many countries send peacekeepers.
Key point: Money and the veto give the US a strong voice in the UN.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: ASEAN's plan for an outward-looking role
questions.question: ASEAN's ________ sets out an outward-looking role for the organisation in the international community.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Vision 2020
Why: ASEAN Vision 2020 defines an outward-looking role for ASEAN, building on its habit of settling disputes by negotiation.
Why not the others:
(A) Agenda 21 came from the 1992 Earth Summit.
(B) Look East is India's policy.
(C) The Maastricht Treaty created the EU.
Key point: ASEAN sees itself playing a wider role in world affairs.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why developing countries backed differentiated responsibilities
questions.question: Why did developing countries argue that the burden of cutting emissions should fall mainly on developed countries?
options: A) Because developing countries have no industries of their own
B) Because developed countries are smaller in area than others
C) Because developed countries caused most of the past emissions
D) Because emissions in developing countries cause no harm at all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because developed countries caused most of the past emissions
Why: Most greenhouse gases accumulated so far came from the industrialised North, so the South argued it should bear more of the burden.
Why not the others:
(A) Developing countries do have industries.
(B) Size is not the argument.
(D) All emissions add to the problem.
Key point: Common but differentiated responsibilities rests on historical emissions.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: India's foreign relations, 1954–1971 — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Panchsheel agreement was signed by Nehru and Zhou Enlai in 1954.
(B) India signed a Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the USSR in August 1971.
(C) The Tashkent Agreement of 1966 was brokered by the President of the United States.
(D) Lal Bahadur Shastri was the Prime Minister during the 1965 war.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the Tashkent Agreement was brokered by the Soviet Union.
Why not the others: (A) Panchsheel was signed in 1954. (B) The Indo-Soviet treaty was signed in August 1971. (D) Shastri led India in 1965. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The USSR, not the US, mediated at Tashkent.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Leaders in the politics of South Asia
questions.question:
Match List-I (Leader) with List-II (Role).

List-I
(A) King Gyanendra
(B) Benazir Bhutto
(C) Sheikh Hasina
(D) Ziaur Rahman

List-II
(I) Military ruler who formed the Bangladesh Nationalist Party
(II) Leader of the Awami League
(III) King of Nepal who dismissed the elected government
(IV) Prime Minister of Pakistan after 1988
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Gyanendra was the king of Nepal who dismissed the government (III). Benazir Bhutto became Pakistan's PM after 1988 (IV). Sheikh Hasina leads the Awami League (II). Ziaur Rahman formed the BNP (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Gyanendra and Benazir. Option (C) swaps Benazir and Hasina. Option (D) swaps Hasina and Ziaur Rahman.
Key point: Democracy in South Asia has faced kings, generals and rival parties.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Punjab in the 1970s and 1980s — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Anandpur Sahib Resolution of 1973 called for regional autonomy.
(B) Operation Blue Star took place in June 1984.
(C) The Rajiv Gandhi–Longowal accord was signed in 1985.
(D) The Punjab accord brought militancy to an immediate end.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. (D) is wrong: violence continued in Punjab for about a decade after the accord.
Why not the others: Option (A) leaves out the true statement (B). Options (C) and (D) include the false statement (D).
Key point: Peace in Punjab came slowly, in the mid-1990s.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Groups that have weakened elected rule in Pakistan
questions.question: According to NCERT, which groups have stood in the way of stable elected government in Pakistan?
options: A) Trade unions, students and the press
B) Foreign NGOs and UN observers
C) The army, the clergy and big landowners
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The army, the clergy and big landowners
Why: The dominance of the military, the clergy and the landowning aristocracy has repeatedly undermined elected governments.
Why not the others:
(A) These groups have usually pushed for democracy.
(B) NCERT does not name them.
(D) These are not the groups NCERT names.
Key point: The social power of these groups has weakened democracy.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Landmarks of global environmental politics
questions.question:
Match List-I (Landmark) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) Earth Summit
(B) Kyoto Protocol
(C) Our Common Future
(D) Limits to Growth

List-II
(I) Set emission targets for industrialised countries
(II) Report of the Club of Rome, 1972
(III) Brundtland Report, 1987
(IV) Held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: The Earth Summit met at Rio in 1992 (IV). The Kyoto Protocol set targets for industrialised countries (I). Our Common Future is the Brundtland Report (III). Limits to Growth was the Club of Rome's report (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the Earth Summit and Kyoto. Option (C) swaps Kyoto and Our Common Future. Option (D) swaps the two reports.
Key point: Concern for the environment grew from the 1970s on.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why the United Front of 1996 relied on the Congress
questions.question: Why did the United Front government formed in 1996 depend on the Congress?
options: A) Because the Congress was a member of its council of ministers
B) Because it survived on the Congress's support from outside
C) Because the Congress President had to approve each of its bills
D) Because the Constitution then required a Congress Prime Minister
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Because it survived on the Congress's support from outside
Why: The United Front did not have a majority of its own and was supported by the Congress from outside.
Why not the others:
(A) The Congress did not join the ministry.
(C) No such approval was needed.
(D) The Constitution has no such rule.
Key point: Outside support made coalition governments fragile.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: What moves least freely under globalisation
questions.question: Under globalisation, which of the following moves across borders LEAST freely?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) People
Why: Developed countries guard their borders with visa rules, so people move far less freely than goods, money or ideas.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) move more freely across borders.
Key point: Borders remain closed to many people even as trade opens.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Why India has built up its military strength
questions.question: Why, according to NCERT, has India sought to strengthen its military capabilities?
options: A) Because it has been involved in conflicts with its neighbours
B) Because it wants to join a Western military alliance
C) Because the UN requires every state to have nuclear arms
D) Because it plans to take over its smaller neighbours
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Because it has been involved in conflicts with its neighbours
Why: India has fought wars with Pakistan and China and faces nuclear-armed neighbours, so it has built up its military.
Why not the others:
(B) India has stayed out of military blocs.
(C) The UN requires nothing of the kind.
(D) India has no such aim.
Key point: Military strength is the first part of India's security strategy.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Style of cooperation among ASEAN members
questions.question: Which description best fits the manner in which ASEAN members conduct their regional affairs, known as the 'ASEAN Way'?
options: A) a single military command for all member states
B) a common currency used across Southeast Asia
C) informal, non-confrontational and cooperative interaction
D) a rule that members follow the decisions of the largest state
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) informal, non-confrontational and cooperative interaction
Why: The ASEAN Way is a style of interaction that is informal, non-confrontational and cooperative, respecting national sovereignty.
Why not the others:
(A) ASEAN has no joint military command.
(B) ASEAN has no common currency.
(D) ASEAN works by consensus.
Key point: ASEAN avoids supranational structures.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Not one of the pillars of the ASEAN Community
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the pillars of the ASEAN Community?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ASEAN Monetary Union
Why: The ASEAN Community rests on security, economic and socio-cultural pillars. There is no monetary union.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are the three pillars.
Key point: ASEAN cooperates without a single currency.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Features of globalisation — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Globalisation involves flows of ideas, capital, commodities and people.
(B) Globalisation has only one cause, which is technology.
(C) India began its economic reforms in 1991.
(D) Critics fear that globalisation may lead to the spread of a uniform culture.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: technology is important, but globalisation has many causes, including political and economic decisions.
Why not the others: (A) Globalisation involves several kinds of flows. (C) India's reforms began in 1991. (D) Critics fear cultural homogenisation. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Globalisation is multi-dimensional and has many causes.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Not a consequence of the Emergency
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a consequence of the Emergency of 1975–77?
options: C) Abolition of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Abolition of the Supreme Court
Why: The Supreme Court continued to exist throughout the Emergency.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) did happen: the press was censored, leaders were jailed and organisations like the RSS were banned.
Key point: The Emergency curbed rights but did not abolish the courts.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Economists and planners of independent India
questions.question:
Match List-I (Person) with List-II (Contribution).

List-I
(A) P.C. Mahalanobis
(B) J.C. Kumarappa
(C) K.N. Raj
(D) Verghese Kurien

List-II
(I) Argued that India should 'hasten slowly' at first
(II) Architect of the Second Five Year Plan
(III) Led the cooperative milk movement in Gujarat
(IV) Gandhian economist who proposed an alternative plan
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Mahalanobis drew up the Second Plan (II). Kumarappa offered a Gandhian alternative (IV). K.N. Raj, who helped draft the First Plan, urged India to 'hasten slowly' (I). Kurien led the Gujarat milk cooperatives (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Mahalanobis and Kumarappa. Option (B) swaps Kumarappa and Raj. Option (C) swaps Raj and Kurien.
Key point: Planning in India drew on many different ideas.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: UN founding and Council terms — spot the true set
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The United Nations came into being on 24 October 1945.
(B) The Secretary-General is appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council.
(C) India was one of the founding members of the UN.
(D) The non-permanent members of the Security Council serve for five years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. (D) is wrong: non-permanent members serve two-year terms.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Non-permanent members of the Council serve two-year terms.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: What India's nuclear doctrine commits it to
questions.question: India's nuclear doctrine commits the country to:
options: A) using nuclear weapons first if attacked by any means
B) no first use of nuclear weapons
C) giving up all its nuclear weapons by a fixed date
D) sharing its nuclear weapons with friendly states
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) no first use of nuclear weapons
Why: India's doctrine states that it will not be the first to use nuclear weapons, while seeking global disarmament.
Why not the others:
(A) That is a first-use policy.
(C) India has set no such deadline.
(D) India does not share its weapons.
Key point: No first use is central to India's nuclear policy.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Where the Afro-Asian conference of 1955 met
questions.question: The Afro-Asian conference held in 1955, in which India played a leading role, met at ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Bandung
Why: The Afro-Asian conference of 1955 was held at Bandung in Indonesia.
Why not the others:
(A) Belgrade hosted the first NAM summit in 1961.
(B) Colombo was not the venue.
(D) Cairo was not the venue.
Key point: Bandung paved the way for the Non-Aligned Movement.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Why the Second Plan raised tariffs on imports
questions.question: Why did the Second Five Year Plan impose high tariffs on imports?
options: A) To protect domestic industries from foreign competition
B) To stop all trade with the countries of the West
C) To raise money for the private sector's exports
D) To bring down the prices of imported machinery
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) To protect domestic industries from foreign competition
Why: High tariffs shielded Indian industries, both public and private, while they grew.
Why not the others:
(B) Trade continued; it was only restricted.
(C) Tariffs taxed imports; they did not fund exports.
(D) Tariffs raise import prices.
Key point: Protection was part of the strategy of rapid industrialisation.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Why Congress dominance in India was unlike one-party rule elsewhere
questions.question: Why is the Congress's dominance in the first decades after independence considered different from one-party rule in countries like China or Cuba?
options: A) Because it existed under free and fair multi-party elections
B) Because the Constitution allowed only one national party
C) Because opposition parties were banned until the year 1977
D) Because the Congress never won a majority in Parliament
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Because it existed under free and fair multi-party elections
Why: In India, the Congress stayed dominant even though other parties were free to compete in democratic elections.
Why not the others:
(B) The Constitution allows any number of parties.
(C) Opposition parties were never banned in this period.
(D) The Congress won large majorities.
Key point: India's one-party dominance was a democratic phenomenon.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Terms and titles of the Emergency years
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) Article 352
(B) MISA
(C) Twenty-Point Programme
(D) Lok Nayak

List-II
(I) Title by which Jayaprakash Narayan was known
(II) Programme announced by the government during the Emergency
(III) Law used to detain people without trial
(IV) Provision under which a national emergency was declared
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Article 352 provides for a national emergency (IV). MISA allowed preventive detention (III). The Twenty-Point Programme was announced during the Emergency (II). JP was called Lok Nayak (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Article 352 and MISA. Option (C) swaps MISA and the Twenty-Point Programme. Option (D) swaps the Twenty-Point Programme and Lok Nayak.
Key point: Preventive detention was the main tool of the Emergency.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Terms from the end of the Soviet system
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Glasnost
(B) Perestroika
(C) Shock therapy
(D) 'The largest garage sale in history'

List-II
(I) Restructuring of the economy
(II) Openness
(III) Sale of state industries at very low prices
(IV) A sudden shift to a capitalist economy
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: Glasnost meant openness (II). Perestroika meant restructuring (I). Shock therapy was the sudden shift to capitalism (IV). The 'garage sale' was the sale of state industries at throwaway prices (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps glasnost and perestroika. Option (B) swaps shock therapy and the garage sale. Option (D) swaps perestroika and shock therapy.
Key point: Reform under Gorbachev was followed by shock therapy after 1991.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Regional events, 1963–1987, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Nagaland becomes a State
(B) Mizoram becomes a State
(C) Sikkim becomes a part of India
(D) The Akali Dal passes the Anandpur Sahib Resolution
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (D), (C), (B)
Why: (A) Nagaland became a State in 1963. (D) The Anandpur Sahib Resolution came in 1973. (C) Sikkim joined India in 1975. (B) Mizoram became a State in 1987.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Sikkim before the resolution. Option (B) puts the resolution before Nagaland. Option (C) puts Mizoram before Sikkim.
Key point: 1963 → 1973 → 1975 → 1987.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Commission that inquired into the Ayodhya demolition
questions.question: The commission appointed to inquire into the circumstances of the demolition at Ayodhya was the ________ Commission.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Liberhan
Why: The Liberhan Commission investigated the events leading to the demolition.
Why not the others:
(B) The Shah Commission looked into the Emergency.
(C) The Mandal Commission dealt with backward classes.
(D) The Sarkaria Commission examined Centre–State relations.
Key point: The Liberhan Commission reported on the 1992 demolition.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: What the Instrument of Accession did
questions.question: What did a ruler agree to by signing the 'Instrument of Accession' in 1947–48?
options: A) To hold a plebiscite in his state within one year
B) That his state would become a part of the Indian Union
C) To remain independent while trading freely with India
D) That his state would be divided between India and Pakistan
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) That his state would become a part of the Indian Union
Why: By signing the Instrument of Accession, a ruler agreed that his state would become part of India.
Why not the others:
(A) A plebiscite was not part of the Instrument.
(C) Independence was the opposite of accession.
(D) Accession meant joining India, not division.
Key point: Most princely states joined India through this document.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Odd one out among the Baltic republics
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the Baltic republics that led the push for independence from the USSR?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Kazakhstan
Why: Kazakhstan is in Central Asia, not on the Baltic Sea.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are the three Baltic republics.
Key point: The Baltic republics were among the first to break away.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Founders and leaders of the early opposition
questions.question:
Match List-I (Leader) with List-II (Party or role).

List-I
(A) Syama Prasad Mookerjee
(B) C. Rajagopalachari
(C) Acharya Narendra Dev
(D) A.K. Gopalan

List-II
(I) Founder of the Swatantra Party
(II) Communist leader from Kerala
(III) Founder of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh
(IV) Founder of the Congress Socialist Party
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Syama Prasad Mookerjee founded the Jana Sangh (III). C. Rajagopalachari founded the Swatantra Party (I). Acharya Narendra Dev founded the Congress Socialist Party (IV). A.K. Gopalan was a communist leader from Kerala (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Rajagopalachari and Narendra Dev. Option (C) swaps Mookerjee and Rajagopalachari. Option (D) swaps Narendra Dev and Gopalan.
Key point: The early opposition was small but led by notable figures.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: What the jeans-and-kurta example shows
questions.question: Young people wearing blue jeans with a khadi kurta is given as an example of:
options: A) the complete replacement of Indian culture
B) the rejection of all foreign influences
C) the mixing of cultures to create something new
D) a law requiring Western dress in colleges
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) the mixing of cultures to create something new
Why: The example shows how outside influences combine with local traditions, a sign of cultural heterogenisation.
Why not the others:
(A) Indian culture is kept, not replaced.
(B) Jeans are a foreign influence that is accepted.
(D) No such law exists.
Key point: Globalisation can enlarge cultural choices as well as narrow them.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Leader of the Naga demand for independence
questions.question: The Naga National Council's struggle for independence was led by ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Angami Zapu Phizo
Why: A.Z. Phizo led the Naga National Council's demand for independence.
Why not the others:
(B) Laldenga led the Mizo National Front.
(C) Sheikh Abdullah was a leader of Kashmir.
(D) Dorji led the democratic movement in Sikkim.
Key point: Phizo led the oldest secessionist movement in the North-East.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Not a part of India's security strategy
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the components of India's security strategy?
options: A) Strengthening international norms and institutions
B) Dealing with internal security challenges
C) Developing the economy to lift people out of poverty
D) Joining a military bloc led by a superpower
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Joining a military bloc led by a superpower
Why: India's strategy has avoided joining military blocs.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C), along with military strength, are the components NCERT lists.
Key point: India's security strategy combines military and non-military means.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Reorganisation of States — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed in 1953.
(B) The States Reorganisation Act was passed in 1956.
(C) Potti Sriramulu died after a long fast for a separate Andhra State.
(D) Nagaland was created as a State under the 1956 Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. (D) is wrong: Nagaland became a State in 1963, not under the 1956 Act.
Why not the others: Option (A) leaves out the true statement (C). Options (B) and (D) include the false statement (D).
Key point: The 1956 Act redrew the map on linguistic lines; more States came later.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: European and Asian integration, 1957–2002, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The European Economic Community is formed
(B) The Maastricht Treaty establishes the European Union
(C) ASEAN is set up by the Bangkok Declaration
(D) Euro notes and coins come into circulation
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (C), (B), (D)
Why: (A) The EEC was formed in 1957. (C) ASEAN was set up in 1967. (B) The Maastricht Treaty came in 1992. (D) Euro notes and coins came into use in 2002.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts ASEAN before the EEC. Options (C) and (D) put the euro before Maastricht.
Key point: 1957 → 1967 → 1992 → 2002.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: When the whole country moved to EVMs
questions.question: By ________, the entire country had shifted to voting through Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2004
Why: EVMs came into use in the 1990s, and by 2004 they were used across the whole country.
Why not the others:
(A) 1952 saw the first election, with a box for each candidate.
(B) Ballot papers with symbols were then in use.
(C) EVMs were not yet in general use.
Key point: The method of voting changed from boxes to ballot papers to EVMs.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Indian policy that mandates cleaner vehicle fuels
questions.question: Which Indian policy requires the use of cleaner fuels for vehicles?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The National Auto-fuel Policy
Why: The National Auto-fuel Policy mandates cleaner fuels for vehicles.
Why not the others:
(B) That act deals with energy efficiency.
(C) That act concerns the power sector.
(D) That policy concerns forests.
Key point: India has taken its own steps to limit pollution.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Weapons treaties and the 9-11 attacks in sequence
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Chemical Weapons Convention is signed
(B) The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty is signed
(C) Terrorists attack New York and Washington
(D) The Biological Weapons Convention is signed
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: (B) The NPT was signed in 1968. (D) The BWC came in 1972. (A) The CWC came in 1992. (C) The attacks took place on 11 September 2001.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the BWC before the NPT. Option (B) puts the CWC before the BWC. Option (D) puts the attacks before the CWC.
Key point: 1968 → 1972 → 1992 → 2001.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Party formed by Jagjivan Ram in 1977
questions.question: Just before the 1977 election, Jagjivan Ram left the Congress and formed the ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Congress for Democracy
Why: Jagjivan Ram formed the Congress for Democracy, which later merged into the Janata Party.
Why not the others:
(A) The Swatantra Party dated from 1959.
(B) The BLD was Charan Singh's party.
(C) Congress (Organisation) was formed after the 1969 split.
Key point: Defections from the Congress strengthened the opposition in 1977.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Prime Ministers, 1989–1999, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in the order in which they took office as Prime Minister:
(A) H.D. Deve Gowda
(B) Chandra Shekhar
(C) V.P. Singh
(D) Atal Behari Vajpayee, at the head of the government formed in 1999
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (B), (A), (D)
Why: (C) V.P. Singh took office in 1989. (B) Chandra Shekhar followed in 1990. (A) Deve Gowda led the United Front from 1996. (D) Vajpayee formed the NDA government in 1999.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Chandra Shekhar before V.P. Singh. Option (B) puts Deve Gowda before Chandra Shekhar. Option (D) puts the 1999 government before Deve Gowda.
Key point: 1989 → 1990 → 1996 → 1999.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Sri Lanka's record despite the ethnic conflict
questions.question: Despite its long ethnic conflict, Sri Lanka has been noted for:
options: A) the largest army in South Asia
C) being the poorest country in the region
D) a high level of human development
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a high level of human development
Why: Sri Lanka has done well on economic growth and human development, and controlled population growth.
Why not the others:
(A) India has the largest army.
(B) Sri Lanka has been a democracy since 1948.
(C) Sri Lanka is among the better-off countries of the region.
Key point: Sri Lanka scores well on human development indicators.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: What made the presidency vacant in 1969
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In 1967 the Congress Working Committee adopted a Ten Point Programme. It included social control of banks, nationalisation of general insurance, a ceiling on urban property and income, public distribution of food grains, land reforms and the provision of house sites to the rural poor. The senior leaders of the party formally approved the programme, but many of them had serious reservations about it. The tension between the Prime Minister and these leaders came into the open in 1969, when the office of the President of India fell vacant on the death of Dr Zakir Hussain. Despite Indira Gandhi's reservations, the party leadership chose N. Sanjeeva Reddy, a long-time political rival of hers, as the official candidate. Indira Gandhi then encouraged the Vice-President, V.V. Giri, to file his nomination as an independent candidate. She also asked the party's members of Parliament and the legislatures to cast a 'conscience vote', that is, to vote as their own judgement told them rather than follow the party's choice. Giri won by a narrow margin. The defeat of the official candidate formalised the split in the party. Indira Gandhi presented the struggle as an ideological one, between progressives who stood for the poor and conservatives who stood for the rich, and this gave her a popular image.

Question: According to the passage, why did the office of the President fall vacant in 1969?
options: A) Dr Zakir Hussain, the President, died in office.
B) V.V. Giri resigned as President to contest again.
C) The President was removed by an impeachment motion.
D) The President stepped down to lead the Congress party.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Dr Zakir Hussain, the President, died in office.
Why: The passage says the office fell vacant on the death of Dr Zakir Hussain.
Why not the others:
(B) Giri was the Vice-President, not the President.
(C) No impeachment is mentioned.
(D) The passage says nothing of the President leading a party.
Key point: Zakir Hussain's death set off the 1969 presidential contest.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of the 'conscience vote' in 1969
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The senior leaders of the party formally approved the programme, but many of them had serious reservations about it. Indira Gandhi then encouraged the Vice-President, V.V. Giri, to file his nomination as an independent candidate. Question: What did Indira Gandhi mean by asking legislators to cast a 'conscience vote'?
options: A) They should stay away from the election altogether.
B) They should vote only for the official party candidate.
C) They should vote by their own judgement, not the party's choice.
D) They should let the Supreme Court decide the result instead.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) They should vote by their own judgement, not the party's choice.
Why: The passage explains that a conscience vote meant voting as their own judgement told them rather than following the party's choice.
Why not the others:
(A) She wanted them to vote, not abstain.
(B) That is the opposite of a conscience vote.
(D) The courts had no such role.
Key point: The conscience vote was a call to defy the official choice.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Why Giri's victory formalised the split
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In 1967 the Congress Working Committee adopted a Ten Point Programme. It included social control of banks, nationalisation of general insurance, a ceiling on urban property and income, public distribution of food grains, land reforms and the provision of house sites to the rural poor. The senior leaders of the party formally approved the programme, but many of them had serious reservations about it. The tension between the Prime Minister and these leaders came into the open in 1969, when the office of the President of India fell vacant on the death of Dr Zakir Hussain. Despite Indira Gandhi's reservations, the party leadership chose N. Sanjeeva Reddy, a long-time political rival of hers, as the official candidate. Indira Gandhi then encouraged the Vice-President, V.V. Giri, to file his nomination as an independent candidate. She also asked the party's members of Parliament and the legislatures to cast a 'conscience vote', that is, to vote as their own judgement told them rather than follow the party's choice. Giri won by a narrow margin. The defeat of the official candidate formalised the split in the party. Indira Gandhi presented the struggle as an ideological one, between progressives who stood for the poor and conservatives who stood for the rich, and this gave her a popular image.

Question: Why, on the basis of the passage, did the defeat of the official candidate formalise the split in the party?
options: A) Because Giri was a member of an opposition party at the time
B) Because the PM had worked openly against her own party's nominee
C) Because the Constitution requires a party to split after such a defeat
D) Because Sanjeeva Reddy then became Prime Minister in her place
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Because the PM had worked openly against her own party's nominee
Why: Indira Gandhi backed Giri against Reddy, the party's own official candidate, so the conflict between the two sides could no longer be contained.
Why not the others:
(A) Giri stood as an independent and was the Vice-President.
(C) The Constitution says nothing of the kind.
(D) Reddy did not become Prime Minister.
Key point: Open defiance of the party's nominee made the division final.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Claim about the 1969 contest the passage contradicts
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In 1967 the Congress Working Committee adopted a Ten Point Programme. It included social control of banks, nationalisation of general insurance, a ceiling on urban property and income, public distribution of food grains, land reforms and the provision of house sites to the rural poor. The senior leaders of the party formally approved the programme, but many of them had serious reservations about it. The tension between the Prime Minister and these leaders came into the open in 1969, when the office of the President of India fell vacant on the death of Dr Zakir Hussain. Despite Indira Gandhi's reservations, the party leadership chose N. Sanjeeva Reddy, a long-time political rival of hers, as the official candidate. Indira Gandhi then encouraged the Vice-President, V.V. Giri, to file his nomination as an independent candidate. She also asked the party's members of Parliament and the legislatures to cast a 'conscience vote', that is, to vote as their own judgement told them rather than follow the party's choice. Giri won by a narrow margin. The defeat of the official candidate formalised the split in the party. Indira Gandhi presented the struggle as an ideological one, between progressives who stood for the poor and conservatives who stood for the rich, and this gave her a popular image.

Question: Which one of these claims is contradicted by what the passage says?
options: A) Giri was the Vice-President when he filed his nomination.
B) Reddy was chosen despite Indira Gandhi's reservations.
C) The senior leaders rejected the Ten Point Programme outright.
D) Indira Gandhi gave the struggle an ideological colour.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The senior leaders rejected the Ten Point Programme outright.
Why: The passage says the senior leaders formally approved the programme, though with reservations, so (C) contradicts it.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are each stated in the passage.
Key point: Approval in form hid disagreement in substance.
